questions.q: Why isn't the training reward curve from lesson 68 a valid evaluation of whether the model actually improved?
options: Because it's always decreasing, not increasing
Because it's measured on training data using the exact reward function the policy is being optimized against, so it confirms optimization is happening but not that the model generalized
Because TRL does not log a reward curve
Because the reward curve only reflects the reference model's performance
questions.explain: The reward curve is a training-time diagnostic on data the policy is actively optimizing against; it doesn't test performance on unseen data.

questions.q: Why is the held-out set from lesson 66 essential for this lesson's evaluation?
options: It isn't essential; any dataset works equally well
Because it was never seen during PPO training, so performance on it reflects genuine generalization rather than fitting to the training distribution or reward function
Because it contains more examples than the training set
Because it was used to compute the KL penalty during training
questions.explain: A valid evaluation needs data the model never trained on; the held-out set carved out in lesson 66 serves exactly that purpose.

questions.q: Why does the pass-rate comparison code use greedy decoding (do_sample=False) for both the baseline and PPO-trained model?
options: Greedy decoding is required by the PPOTrainer API
So that any difference in pass rate reflects the actual policy change rather than random sampling variance between generation runs
Greedy decoding always produces longer responses
It is not actually necessary and is only a stylistic choice
questions.explain: Using sampling for one model and not the other (or random sampling for both) would introduce noise unrelated to the actual policy improvement being measured.

questions.q: A capstone project shows the PPO model's pass rate improved 15 points over baseline on the held-out set. According to this lesson, what should happen next before declaring success?
options: Nothing further is needed; the pass-rate number is sufficient on its own
Immediately retrain with a higher learning rate
Read a sample of the PPO model's actual generations and compare response-length distributions, to check the improvement isn't a reward-hacking artifact or degenerate shortcut
Discard the held-out set and re-evaluate on the training set instead
questions.explain: A pass-rate improvement alone can hide reward hacking or degenerate outputs; this lesson recommends manually inspecting generations and length distributions before trusting the number.

questions.q: What would be a warning sign, during evaluation, that the PPO model's pass-rate gain is a gamed shortcut rather than genuine improvement?
options: The PPO model's reasoning remains coherent and its response lengths are similar to baseline

The PPO model shows a sharply different response-length distribution and/or reasoning that looks degenerate despite landing on correct-looking answers, echoing the reward-hacking exploit described in lesson 67
The PPO model's pass rate exactly matches the baseline's
The evaluation was run with greedy decoding on both models
questions.explain: Degenerate or format-exploiting generations that still score well on the verifier are the concrete sign of reward hacking that a pass-rate number alone would miss.
